modules.title: What is Version Control? Introducing Git
modules.content:
## A Story Without a Safety Net Imagine you’re writing the first chapter of a novel on a shared computer. You type a paragraph, hit **Save**, and hand the file to a colleague. An hour later you discover that the paragraph you just added has been overwritten by an older version someone else saved earlier. You scramble through backup copies, email threads, and a few printed drafts, but the exact wording you loved is gone forever. Now picture the same scenario with a simple tool that records every change you make, lets you travel back in time, and lets multiple writers work side‑by‑side without stepping on each other’s toes. That tool is a **version control system (VCS)**, and Git is the most widely‑used VCS today. --- ## What Is Version Control? A version control system is software that **records the history of changes** to files (or sets of files) over time. Each time you tell the system to “save” a snapshot, it creates a new, immutable record that you can later retrieve, compare, or roll back to. ### Core Idea in Plain Language - **Snapshot** – Think of a photograph of your project at a particular moment. - **History** – A chronological album of those photographs, each labeled with when it was taken and why. - **Restore** – The ability to replace the current view of your project with any earlier photograph. ### Why Do We Need It? | Situation | Without VCS | With VCS | |-----------|--------------|----------| | **Accidental deletion** | File disappears forever or you must dig through backups. | Retrieve the deleted file from the previous snapshot instantly. | | **Multiple contributors** | Overwrites, lost work, endless “who has the latest version?” emails. | Each change is tracked, merged safely, and attributed to its author. | | **Experimenting** | Fear of breaking the project; you may avoid trying new ideas. | Create a separate line of development (a *branch*) and discard it without harm. | | **Audit & accountability** | Hard to know who changed what and why. | Every change is logged with author, timestamp, and an optional message. | | **Release management** | No clear way to package a specific state for deployment. | Tag a particular commit as a release, guaranteeing reproducibility. | These benefits translate into **greater confidence**, **faster collaboration**, and **more reliable software**—or any collection of files, for that matter. --- ## Centralized vs. Distributed Version Control Version control systems come in two broad families. Understanding the difference helps explain why Git’s distributed model has become dominant. ### 1. Centralized Version Control Systems (CVCS) A centralized system relies on a **single, authoritative server** that holds the master copy of the project. Developers *check out* files, edit them locally, and then *commit* their changes back to the central server. #### Classic Examples - **CVS** (Concurrent Versions System) – early 1990s. - **Subversion (SVN)** – popular in the 2000s. #### How It Works (Simplified Flow) 1. **Checkout** a working copy from the central repository. 2. **Edit** files locally. 3. **Commit** changes back to the central server. 4. **Update** your local copy to incorporate others’ commits. #### Advantages - **Simple mental model** – “One place, one source of truth.” - **Easy access control** – Administrators can manage permissions centrally. #### Drawbacks - **Network dependency** – You cannot commit or view history without a connection to the server. - **Single point of failure** – If the server crashes, the entire team is blocked. - **Limited offline work** – Developers can only view the latest snapshot; they cannot create private histories. ### 2. Distributed Version Control Systems (DVCS) A distributed system, like Git, gives **every clone a full copy of the entire repository**, including its complete history. There is no single “central” server; any clone can act as a source for others. #### Popular Examples - **Git** – created in 2005 for the Linux kernel. - **Mercurial** – another DVCS, similar in philosophy. #### How It Works (Simplified Flow) 1. **Clone** a repository – you receive the whole history. 2. **Commit** locally – changes are saved in your private copy. 3. **Push** or **pull** – exchange commits with other clones when you choose. #### Advantages - **Full offline capability** – you can view history, create branches, and commit without any network. - **Robustness** – If any server fails, any clone can become the new source. - **Flexible workflows** – Teams can adopt centralized, peer‑to‑peer, or hybrid models. #### Drawbacks - **Initial clone size** – The first download can be larger because it includes the whole history. - **Steeper learning curve** – Concepts like *push*, *pull*, and *rebasing* can be confusing at first. ### Why Git Won the Race Git combines **speed**, **data integrity**, and **flexible branching** with a **tiny footprint** for each commit (thanks to clever storage of changes). Its design, originally crafted for a project with thousands of contributors spread around the globe, makes it uniquely suited for both solo developers and massive open‑source communities. --- ## Core Git Terminology (First Encounter) When you start using Git, you’ll repeatedly see a handful of words. Knowing them early prevents confusion later. ### Repository (Repo) A **repository** is the container that holds **all** of your project’s files **and** the complete history of every change. Think of it as the “photo album” for your code. - **Local repository** – The copy on your own computer. - **Remote repository** – A copy hosted on a server (e.g., GitHub, GitLab) that you can share with others. ### Working Directory (or Working Tree) The **working directory** is the set of files you see on disk and edit day‑to‑day. It reflects the state of a particular commit (often the latest one you checked out). ### Commit A **commit** is a **snapshot** of the entire project at a given moment, together with a **commit message** that explains *why* the change was made. Commits form a chain, each pointing to its predecessor, creating the project’s history. - **Commit hash** – A unique 40‑character identifier (e.g., `a1b2c3d4…`) generated from the commit’s contents. - **Commit message** – A short description (ideally imperative, like “Fix login bug”) that helps others understand the purpose of the change. ### Branch A **branch** is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. It allows you to diverge from the main line of development, work on a feature or experiment, and later bring those changes back together. - **`main` (or `master`)** – The default branch that usually represents the stable, release‑ready code. - **Feature branch** – A temporary branch named after the work you’re doing (e.g., `feature/login-form`). ### Staging Area (Index) Before a commit is created, Git lets you **stage** individual changes. The staging area is a *pre‑commit* holding pen where you assemble exactly what will go into the next snapshot. (We’ll explore staging in depth later, but the term will appear now.) ### Remote A **remote** is a shorthand name for a repository that lives somewhere else (often on a server). The most common remote name is `origin`, which usually points to the primary shared repository. --- ## Real‑World Snapshots: Seeing the Concepts in Action ### Example 1 – A Solo Writer Using Git Locally *Anna* is drafting a short story. She creates a folder `my‑novel/` and runs `git init` (we’ll cover that command later). 1. **First draft** – She writes the opening paragraph, stages the file (`git add .`), and commits (`git commit -m "Add opening paragraph"`). 2. **Revising** – After a week, she rewrites the opening to be more compelling. She stages the changes and makes a new commit: `git commit -m "Rewrite opening for stronger hook"`. 3. **Accidental deletion** – She accidentally deletes the file. By running `git checkout HEAD -- opening.txt`, she restores the latest version instantly. *What she experienced*: each commit acted as a safety net, and the entire history lived on her laptop—no server required. ### Example 2 – A Small Team Comparing Centralized vs. Distributed Workflows A three‑person team, **Beta**, builds a simple website. | Workflow | Steps | What Happens If the Server Goes Down? | |----------|-------|----------------------------------------| | **Centralized (SVN)** | 1. Checkout from central repo.
2. Edit locally.
3. Commit back to central repo.
4. Update to get teammates’ changes. | **Blocked** – No commit or update possible until the server is back. | | **Distributed (Git)** | 1. Clone the repo (full history).
2. Commit locally (no network needed).
3. When online, push commits to a shared remote.
4. Pull teammates’ pushes when convenient. | **Unblocked** – Team members continue committing locally; they can later push/pull once the server is restored. | Beta quickly notices that with Git they can **work offline on a train**, create experimental branches, and still keep a single source of truth once they reconnect. This flexibility is why many small teams migrate from SVN to Git. ### Example 3 – An Open‑Source Project’s Public History The popular JavaScript library **Lodash** lives on GitHub. Its repository contains **hundreds of thousands of commits** from contributors worldwide. Each commit carries: - **Author name** – Who wrote the change. - **Timestamp** – When it was added. - **Message** – Why the change was made. Anyone can **clone** the entire history, explore how a particular function evolved, or **checkout** a specific release tag (e.g., `v4.17.21`) to reproduce the exact code used in production. The public nature of the repository also enables **code review**, **issue tracking**, and **fork‑based contributions**, all built on top of the same Git fundamentals introduced here. --- ## Why Git Is the De‑Facto Choice for Modern Development 1. **Speed** – Git’s internal data structures (like *packfiles* and *hash‑based objects*) make operations such as committing, branching, and merging **instantaneous**, even on large codebases. 2. **Branching as a First‑Class Citizen** – Creating a new branch is a single‑line command and takes only a few milliseconds. This encourages developers to use branches for every small task, leading to cleaner, more isolated changes. 3. **Data Integrity** – Every object (commits, trees, blobs) is identified by a **SHA‑1 hash** of its contents. If any file is corrupted, Git will detect it immediately, protecting the repository from silent damage. 4. **Distributed Nature** – Because each clone is a full backup, the risk of losing the entire project to a server crash is dramatically reduced. 5. **Ecosystem & Tooling** – Platforms like **GitHub**, **GitLab**, and **Bitbucket** provide web‑based interfaces, issue trackers, and CI/CD pipelines that all assume a Git backend. 6. **Community Support** – With billions of lines of code managed by Git, the community has produced countless tutorials, plugins, and best‑practice guides—making learning and troubleshooting easier for beginners. These factors combine to make Git not just a version control system, but a **collaboration platform** that scales from a single developer’s laptop to the world’s largest open‑source projects. --- ## Putting the Pieces Together - **Version control** records every change, allowing you to travel back in time, compare versions, and collaborate without conflict. - **Centralized VCS** rely on a single server; they’re simple but fragile and limit offline work. - **Distributed VCS**, exemplified by **Git**, give each user a complete copy of the project, enabling robust, flexible, and fast workflows. - The **key Git terms** you’ll meet from now on are **repository**, **commit**, **branch**, **working directory**, **staging area**, and **remote**. Understanding these concepts will let you start using Git confidently in the upcoming chapters. --- ## Key Takeaways - A **version control system** is a tool that snapshots and tracks changes to files over time, providing safety, accountability, and collaboration capabilities. - **Benefits** include loss prevention, easy collaboration, experimental branching, audit trails, and reproducible releases. - **Centralized VCS** (e.g., SVN) depend on a single server; **distributed VCS** (e.g., Git) give every user a full copy of the repository, allowing offline work and greater resilience. - In Git, the fundamental concepts are: - **Repository** – the container for all files and their history. - **Commit** – a permanent snapshot with a descriptive message. - **Branch** – a lightweight pointer enabling parallel development. - **Working directory**, **staging area**, and **remote** – the surrounding context for making and sharing changes. - Git’s speed, robust branching, data integrity, and thriving ecosystem make it the go‑to VCS for individuals and teams alike. With these foundations, you’re ready to install Git, create your first repository, and start capturing your own development history.

modules.content:
## A First‑Day Project: Why You Need Git Right Now  

Imagine you have just finished writing the first draft of a short story on your laptop. You hit **Save**, close the file, and later discover that a stray keystroke corrupted the only copy you have. Panic sets in—there’s no way to recover the lost paragraphs.  

Now picture the same scenario, but you had **Git** installed and had committed your work after each paragraph. By simply running a Git command, you could roll back to the previous, untouched version and continue writing without missing a beat. This is the everyday power Git gives you, even before you start collaborating with others.

In this chapter you’ll get Git onto your computer, tell it who you are, and set a few sensible defaults so that your first commit feels natural. No prior command‑line experience is required.

---

## 1. Downloading and Installing Git  

### 1.1 Windows  

1. **Visit the official installer** – open your browser and go to <https://git-scm.com/download/win>. The download should start automatically.  
2. **Run the installer** – double‑click the downloaded `Git-2.xx.x‑64-bit.exe`.  
3. **Wizard steps (keep the defaults unless you have a reason to change them)**  

   * **Select Components** – leave all boxes checked.  
   * **Path environment** – choose “Git from the command line and also from 3rd‑party software”. This adds `git` to your system’s `PATH` so you can type `git` in any Command Prompt or PowerShell window.  
   * **Choosing the SSH client** – the default “OpenSSH” works for most users.  
   * **Line ending conversions** – select **“Checkout Windows‑style, commit Unix‑style line endings”** (the safest default).  
   * **Default editor** – the installer suggests **Vim**; you can change this later (see §4).  

4. **Finish** – click *Install* and then *Finish*. Git Bash—a lightweight terminal that ships with Git—will be available from the Start menu.

> **Example:** After installation, open *Git Bash* and type `git --version`. You should see something like `git version 2.41.0.windows.1`. If you see the version number, Git is ready to use.

### 1.2 macOS  

macOS already includes a minimal version of Git as part of the Xcode command‑line tools, but it’s often outdated. Follow one of the two approaches below.

#### Option A – Using the official installer  

1. Download the macOS package from <https://git-scm.com/download/mac>.  
2. Open the `.dmg` file and drag the **Git** icon into your *Applications* folder.  
3. Open *Terminal* (found in **Applications → Utilities**) and run `git --version` to confirm the installation.

#### Option B – Using Homebrew (recommended for developers)

1. If you don’t have Homebrew, install it first:  

   ```bash
   /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
   ```

2. Then install Git:  

   ```bash
   brew install git
   ```

3. Verify with `git --version`.

> **Example:** After installing via Homebrew, the command `git config --list --show-origin` will show you where Git reads its configuration files from, confirming that the tool is correctly set up.

### 1.3 Linux  

Most Linux distributions ship with Git in their default repositories.

| Distribution | Command |
|--------------|---------|
| Ubuntu / Debian | `sudo apt update && sudo apt install git` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install git` |
| Arch Linux | `sudo pacman -S git` |
| openSUSE | `sudo zypper install git` |

Run the appropriate command for your distro, then type `git --version` to verify.

> **Example:** On Ubuntu, after installation you might see `git version 2.34.1`. If the version appears, you’re good to go.

---

## 2. Setting Your Identity Globally  

Every commit you create records **who** made the change. Git stores this information in two configuration variables: `user.name` and `user.email`. Setting them **globally** means they apply to every repository on your machine, unless you override them locally later.

### 2.1 The `git config` command  

Open a terminal (Command Prompt, PowerShell, Git Bash, or macOS/Linux Terminal) and run:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Full Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

* **`--global`** – tells Git to write the settings to the global config file (`~/.gitconfig` on macOS/Linux, `%USERPROFILE%\.gitconfig` on Windows).  
* **`user.name`** – the display name that will appear in commit logs.  
* **`user.email`** – the email address associated with the commit. Many hosting services (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) use this to link commits to your user account.

> **Tip:** Use the same email you will use on your remote‑hosting service; otherwise your contributions may not be linked to your profile.

### 2.2 Verify your configuration  

```bash
git config --global --list
```

You should see something like:

```
user.name=Your Full Name
user.email=you@example.com
```

If you need to edit the file directly, you can open `~/.gitconfig` in any text editor; it follows a simple INI‑style syntax.

---

## 3. Quick Verification: Your First Git Command  

Now that Git is installed and your identity is set, confirm everything works with a harmless command:

```bash
git help
```

This prints a short help summary and, more importantly, confirms that Git can locate its configuration files and run without error.

### 3.1 A tiny test repository  

1. Create a new folder:

   ```bash
   mkdir demo-git
   cd demo-git
   ```

2. Initialise an empty repository:

   ```bash
   git init
   ```

3. Create a file and commit it:

   ```bash
   echo "Hello, Git!" > hello.txt
   git add hello.txt
   git commit -m "Initial commit"
   ```

4. View the log:

   ```bash
   git log --oneline
   ```

You should see a single line with a hash and the message “Initial commit”. The author line will show the name and email you configured earlier. This tiny workflow demonstrates the core cycle of **Edit → Add → Commit** that you will repeat throughout the book.

---

## 4. Common Global Preferences  

Beyond identity, a few settings make Git behave more predictably across platforms.

### 4.1 Line ending handling  

Different operating systems represent line endings differently:

* **Windows** – Carriage Return + Line Feed (`CRLF`)  
* **Unix/macOS** – Line Feed only (`LF`)

If you work on a project that will be shared with developers on other platforms, you want Git to **store** line endings in a consistent format (usually `LF`) while presenting them in the native format for your OS. The setting is `core.autocrlf`.

| OS | Recommended setting |
|----|----------------------|
| Windows | `git config --global core.autocrlf true` |
| macOS / Linux | `git config --global core.autocrlf input` |

* `true` – converts `LF` to `CRLF` on checkout, and back to `LF` on commit.  
* `input` – leaves files untouched on checkout, but converts `CRLF` to `LF` on commit.  

### 4.2 Default editor  

When you run `git commit` without `-m`, Git opens a text editor so you can write a multi‑line commit message. The installer may default to **Vim**, which can be intimidating for beginners. You can set a more familiar editor, such as **Visual Studio Code**, **Notepad++**, or **nano**.

* **VS Code (cross‑platform)**  

  ```bash
  git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
  ```

* **Notepad++ (Windows only)**  

  ```bash
  git config --global core.editor "'C:/Program Files/Notepad++/notepad++.exe' -multiInst -nosession"
  ```

* **nano (macOS/Linux)** – often already installed  

  ```bash
  git config --global core.editor "nano"
  ```

The `--wait` flag (or its equivalent) tells the editor to pause Git until you close the editor window, ensuring the commit proceeds only after you finish writing the message.

### 4.3 Colour output  

Seeing Git’s output colour‑coded (e.g., red for deletions, green for additions) speeds up scanning the terminal. Enable it globally with:

```bash
git config --global color.ui auto
```

### 4.4 Summary of the preferred global settings  

```bash
# Windows line ending handling
git config --global core.autocrlf true

# macOS / Linux line ending handling
# git config --global core.autocrlf input

# Choose your favourite editor (example: VS Code)
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

# Enable colourised output
git config --global color.ui auto
```

You can always check the current values with `git config --global --list`.

---

## 5. Real‑World Scenarios  

### 5.1 Scenario A – A student working on a class project from a Windows laptop  

* **Problem:** The project will be submitted to a Linux‑based grading server.  
* **Solution:** Install Git with the default Windows installer, set `core.autocrlf true` (the installer already does this), and configure the editor to **VS Code** for comfortable commit messages. The line‑ending conversion ensures the submitted files have the correct `LF` endings.

### 5.2 Scenario B – A hobbyist developer using a MacBook and a Raspberry Pi (Linux)  

* **Problem:** The same repository will be edited on both machines, and the developer prefers the lightweight **nano** editor on the Pi.  
* **Solution:** Install Git via Homebrew on macOS and via `apt` on the Pi. Set `core.autocrlf input` on both systems, and configure `core.editor` individually (`code --wait` on macOS, `nano` on the Pi). Because the settings are stored per‑machine, each platform gets the editor that feels natural.

### 5.3 Scenario C – A non‑technical writer who only needs version control for personal documents  

* **Problem:** The writer wants a simple “Save → Commit” button in a graphical Git client but is uncomfortable with the command line.  
* **Solution:** Install Git using the Windows installer, accept the default settings, and then download a GUI client such as **GitHub Desktop**. The global configuration you performed (name/email) will be automatically imported, so the first time they click *Commit* the author fields are already filled.

---

## 6. Troubleshooting Common Issues  

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----------|
| `git` not recognized as a command | `PATH` does not include Git’s binary directory (Windows) | Re‑run the installer and ensure “Git from the command line” is selected, or manually add `C:\Program Files\Git\cmd` to your system `PATH`. |
| `git --version` shows an old version after installing from the website | An older Git binary is earlier in the `PATH` (e.g., from Xcode tools) | Remove the older Git from the `PATH` or uninstall it, then verify the correct binary is first. |
| Commit author shows a different email than expected | Global config not set, or a local repository overrides it | Run `git config --global --list` to confirm values, then `git config --local --list` inside the repo to see overrides. |
| Files appear with mixed line endings after cloning a repo | `core.autocrlf` set incorrectly for the OS | Adjust the setting (`true` on Windows, `input` on macOS/Linux) and re‑clone the repository. |

---

## 7. Next Steps  

Now that Git is installed, your identity is recorded, and sensible defaults are in place, you are ready to **create** and **inspect** local repositories (the focus of the next chapter). Every command you run from here on will be built on the foundation you just set up.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Install Git** using the official installers for Windows/macOS or the package manager for Linux. Verify the installation with `git --version`.  
- **Configure your identity globally** with `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`; this metadata appears in every commit.  
- **Test the setup** by initializing a tiny repository, adding a file, and committing it. The `git log` output confirms that Git records your author information.  
- **Set useful global preferences**:  
  * `core.autocrlf` to handle line endings across platforms,  
  * `core.editor` to choose a comfortable commit‑message editor,  
  * `color.ui` for colour‑coded terminal output.  
- **Troubleshoot** common pitfalls such as missing PATH entries or unexpected line‑ending conversions.  

With Git now a part of your development toolbox, you can move confidently into creating repositories, tracking changes, and eventually collaborating with others. Happy committing!

## A Fresh Start: Turning a Simple Folder into a Full‑Featured Project

Imagine you have just created a folder called **`my‑journal`** on your laptop. Inside, you’ve dropped a plain‑text file `2024‑07‑28.txt` where you jot down ideas for a short story. So far it’s just a collection of files on your hard drive—nothing more, nothing less.  

Now you wonder: *What if I lose this folder?* *What if I later want to look back at earlier drafts?* *What if I decide to share the story with a friend and keep track of every revision?*  

The answer is to turn that ordinary folder into a **Git repository**. By doing so you instantly gain a **local, self‑contained history** of every change you make, without needing any servers or collaborators yet. The moment you run a single command, Git creates a hidden **`.git`** directory that will quietly record every snapshot you take. From there, adding files, checking the current state, and preparing for the first commit become routine tasks.

Below we walk through exactly that process—initializing a repository, adding files, and inspecting the repository’s status—while demystifying the **working directory**, **staging area**, and the mysterious **`.git`** folder.

---

## Initializing a New Repository

### The `git init` Command

The very first step is to tell Git, “This folder is now a repository.” The command is:

```bash
git init
```

Running this inside `my-journal` creates a **new Git repository** *in place*. Git does not move or copy any of your existing files; it merely creates a hidden folder named **`.git`** that will store all the metadata, objects, and configuration needed to track changes.

> **Why “init”?**  
> The verb “initialize” is short for “set up the initial data structures.” In the earlier chapter on *Installing Git and Initial Configuration* you learned that Git is a **distributed version control system (VCS)**. `git init` is the local counterpart of creating a new project on a remote server—it establishes the *authoritative* source of truth for your project on your own machine.

### What Happens Inside `.git`?

The hidden `.git` directory is the heart of every repository. Although you normally never need to look inside it, understanding its purpose helps demystify many later commands.

| Sub‑folder / file | Purpose |
|-------------------|---------|
| `objects/` | Stores **snapshots** (called *objects*) of file contents, identified by SHA‑1 hashes. |
| `refs/` | Holds pointers to the **heads** of branches (e.g., `refs/heads/main`). |
| `HEAD` | A tiny file that tells Git which branch you’re currently on. |
| `config` | Local configuration overrides (e.g., user name, email, merge settings). |
| `index` | The **staging area** (also called the *cache*) that records which files are ready to be committed. |

Because the folder name begins with a dot (`.`), most operating systems treat it as **hidden**. You can reveal it with `ls -a` (Unix/macOS) or `dir /a` (Windows), but you generally let Git manage its contents.

> **Tip:** Never edit files inside `.git` manually unless you know exactly what you’re doing. Corrupting this folder can break the entire repository.

---

## The Three Zones: Working Directory, Staging Area, and Repository

Git separates the life of a file into three distinct zones. Visualizing these zones helps you understand what each command does.

```
+-------------------+       +-------------------+       +-------------------+
| Working Directory | <---> | Staging Area (   | <---> | Repository (.git) |
|   (your files)    |  add  |   index)          | commit|   (history)       |
+-------------------+       +-------------------+       +-------------------+
```

1. **Working Directory** – The files you see on disk. They can be edited, renamed, or deleted at any time.  
2. **Staging Area** – A hidden snapshot of *exactly* what will be committed next. `git add` copies file contents from the working directory into this area.  
3. **Repository** – The permanent, immutable history stored inside `.git`. Each commit adds a new snapshot to this history.

When you first run `git init`, the staging area exists (the `index` file) but is empty. No files are tracked yet.

---

## Adding Files to the Staging Area

### The `git add` Command

To tell Git, “I want this file (or set of files) to be part of the next snapshot,” you use:

```bash
git add <pathspec>
```

- **Single file** – `git add 2024-07-28.txt`  
- **All files** – `git add .` (the dot means “the current directory and everything under it”)  
- **Pattern matching** – `git add *.txt` adds all text files in the current folder.  

When you run `git add`, Git copies the **current content** of the specified files into the staging area. Subsequent edits to those files do **not** affect the staged version until you run `git add` again.

> **Important:** Adding a file does **not** create a commit. It merely prepares the file for the next commit. The actual snapshot is created later with `git commit`.

### Ignoring Unwanted Files

Often a project contains temporary or generated files you never want to track (e.g., editor swap files, compiled binaries). Git respects a special file named **`.gitignore`** that lists patterns to exclude from `git add`. Creating a `.gitignore` is optional at this stage, but you’ll encounter it frequently later on.

Example `.gitignore` for a journal project:

```
# Ignore backup files created by editors
*~
*.bak
```

---

## Inspecting Repository State with `git status`

After initializing a repository and adding files, you’ll frequently need to ask Git, “What is the current state of my project?” The answer comes from:

```bash
git status
```

The output is human‑readable and tells you three things:

1. **Branch information** – Which branch you’re on (by default `master` or `main`).  
2. **Staged changes** – Files that are ready to be committed (the *green* list).  
3. **Unstaged changes** – Files that have been modified but not yet staged (the *red* list).  
4. **Untracked files** – Files Git has never seen before (the *orange* list).

### Typical `git status` Output

```text
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   2024-07-28.txt

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        drafts/
        notes.md
```

- **“Changes to be committed”** – These are the files you have added (`git add`).  
- **“Untracked files”** – Git sees them on disk but you haven’t told it to track them yet.  

If you modify a staged file after running `git add`, you’ll see it appear under **“Changes not staged for commit”** as well, reminding you to re‑add it if you want the latest version in the next commit.

---

## Hands‑On Walkthrough: From Empty Folder to Ready‑to‑Commit

Below is a step‑by‑step illustration using the `my-journal` folder. Feel free to type the commands yourself in a terminal.

1. **Create the folder and a sample file**

   ```bash
   mkdir my-journal
   cd my-journal
   echo "First entry – ideas for a sci‑fi short story." > 2024-07-28.txt
   ```

2. **Initialize the repository**

   ```bash
   git init
   ```

   *Output (shortened)*

   ```
   Initialized empty Git repository in /home/user/my-journal/.git/
   ```

3. **Check the status right away**

   ```bash
   git status
   ```

   *Output*

   ```
   On branch master

   No commits yet

   Untracked files:
     (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
           2024-07-28.txt
   ```

   The file is **untracked** because we haven’t added it yet.

4. **Stage the file**

   ```bash
   git add 2024-07-28.txt
   ```

5. **Verify the staging area**

   ```bash
   git status
   ```

   *Output*

   ```
   On branch master

   No commits yet

   Changes to be committed:
     (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
           new file:   2024-07-28.txt
   ```

   Now the file appears under **“Changes to be committed.”** It is staged and ready for the first commit.

6. **Make a small edit and see the impact**

   ```bash
   echo "Added a twist: the protagonist discovers a hidden portal." >> 2024-07-28.txt
   git status
   ```

   *Output*

   ```
   On branch master

   No commits yet

   Changes to be committed:
     (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
           new file:   2024-07-28.txt

   Changes not staged for commit:
     (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
     (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
           modified:   2024-07-28.txt
   ```

   The file is **both staged and modified**. If you want the newest version to be part of the upcoming commit, run `git add 2024-07-28.txt` again.

---

## Real‑World Example 1: A Solo Project Becomes Versioned

*Scenario*: Maya is writing a personal finance tracker in Python. She creates a folder `finance‑tracker` and drops three files: `main.py`, `requirements.txt`, and `README.md`. She wants to start tracking changes from day one.

**Steps Maya follows**

| Action | Command | Reason |
|--------|---------|--------|
| Initialize repository | `git init` | Creates `.git` and marks the folder as a repo. |
| Stage all existing files | `git add .` | Quickly adds every file in the folder. |
| Verify status | `git status` | Confirms that all three files are staged and ready. |
| (Later) Add a new helper script | `touch utils.py` → `git add utils.py` | Stages the newly created file. |

By the end of the first day, Maya can run `git log` (once she makes a commit) and see a clean snapshot of her codebase—no fear of losing work if her laptop crashes.

---

## Real‑World Example 2: Experimenting with a Configuration File

*Scenario*: Leo is tweaking a `config.yaml` for a web service. He wants to keep each variation in history without committing yet.

**Workflow**

1. `git init` – creates a repository for the config folder.  
2. `git add config.yaml` – stages the original version.  
3. `git commit -m "Initial config"` – (the next chapter will cover committing).  
4. Edit `config.yaml` → `git status` shows **“modified: config.yaml”** under *unstaged*.  
5. If the change is experimental, Leo runs `git add config.yaml` to stage it, then `git commit -m "Try new timeout"` later.  
6. To revert the experimental change before committing, `git restore config.yaml` discards the edit, returning to the last staged version.

This example highlights the **staging area** as a safe sandbox: you can stage a change, review it with `git diff --staged`, and decide whether to keep it.

---

## Real‑World Example 3: Turning an Existing Project into a Repository

*Scenario*: Priya inherited a legacy folder `old‑website/` that contains HTML, CSS, and a handful of images. The folder already has many files, but no Git history.

**Steps**

```bash
cd old-website
git init                     # Turn the existing folder into a repo
git add *.html *.css img/*  # Add only the files she wants to track
git status                   # Verify everything is staged
```

Priya can now start committing from this point forward, gaining version control without moving files around. The existing files become the *first snapshot* of the repository.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

| Pitfall | What Happens | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Forgetting to run `git add` after editing a file | `git status` shows the file under *“Changes not staged for commit”*; the next commit will not include the edit. | Re‑run `git add <file>` before committing. |
| Accidentally adding a large generated directory (e.g., `node_modules/`) | Repository size balloons; future clones become slow. | Add a `.gitignore` entry (`node_modules/`) and remove the directory from the index with `git rm -r --cached node_modules`. |
| Confusing the hidden `.git` folder with regular files | Deleting or moving `.git` destroys the repository. | Never edit or delete `.git` manually; treat it as Git’s private data store. |
| Running `git init` inside a subfolder unintentionally | You end up with a nested repository; Git will ignore files outside the inner `.git`. | Delete the unwanted inner `.git` (`rm -rf .git`) and re‑run `git init` at the intended root. |

---

## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

| Goal | Command | Typical Output |
|------|---------|----------------|
| Create a new repo | `git init` | “Initialized empty Git repository in …/.git/” |
| Stage a single file | `git add filename` | No output (silent success) |
| Stage everything | `git add .` | No output |
| See current state | `git status` | Lists branch, staged, unstaged, and untracked files |
| List ignored files | `git status --ignored` | Shows files matching `.gitignore` patterns |
| Show staged changes (diff) | `git diff --staged` | Diff of what will be committed |

---

## Putting It All Together

By now you should feel comfortable with the **three‑step cycle** that underpins every Git workflow:

1. **Initialize** (`git init`) – Turn any folder into a repository, creating the hidden `.git` directory.  
2. **Stage** (`git add`) – Choose which files (or parts of files) you want to include in the next snapshot.  
3. **Inspect** (`git status`) – Ask Git for a clear, human‑readable report of what is staged, what is modified, and what is still unknown to Git.

These steps are the foundation for the next chapter, where you’ll learn how to **commit** the staged snapshot and start building a navigable history of your project.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **`git init`** converts any directory into a local Git repository by creating a hidden **`.git`** folder that houses all version‑control data.  
- The **working directory**, **staging area**, and **repository** are three distinct zones; understanding their roles prevents accidental loss of work.  
- **`git add`** moves file contents from the working directory into the staging area. Only staged files will be part of the next commit.  
- **`git status`** is your daily diagnostic tool—it tells you which files are untracked, staged, or modified but not yet staged.  
- The **`.git`** folder is hidden for a reason: treat it as Git’s private storage; never edit its contents manually.  
- Real‑world scenarios—solo projects, experimental tweaks, and retro‑fitting existing codebases—benefit from the same simple steps: init → add → status → (later) commit.  

With these basics mastered, you now have a solid, hands‑on foundation for managing any project locally with Git. The next step is to learn how to **commit** your staged changes and start building a reliable history you can explore and, if needed, roll back to. Happy tracking!

modules.content:
## A Real‑World Moment: “Did I Really Save That Fix?”

Imagine you’ve just corrected a typo in `README.md` and added a new feature flag to `config.py`. You run the program, it works, and you feel a surge of confidence—*until* your laptop crashes. When you power it back on, the file you just edited is back to its previous state. What went wrong?  

You never told Git to **record** the changes. In Git, merely editing a file does not automatically create a new snapshot. You must **stage** the modifications and then **commit** them. Once you’ve done that, you can look back at every saved state, compare versions, and never lose work again.

Below we walk through the three core actions you need to master at this stage of your Git journey:

1. **Stage** the changes you want to keep (`git add`).
2. **Commit** those staged changes with a clear, descriptive message (`git commit`).
3. **Explore** the history you’ve built (`git log`) and **compare** snapshots (`git diff`).

---

## 1. Staging Changes – The “Holding Pen” for Your Edits  

When you modify files, Git records the *difference* in a hidden area called the **staging area** (also known as the **index**). Think of it as a “holding pen” where you decide which changes belong together in the next snapshot.

### 1.1 Adding Files to the Staging Area  

The most common way to stage is with `git add`. It tells Git, “These changes are ready to be committed.”

```bash
# Stage a single file
git add README.md

# Stage multiple files at once
git add config.py utils.py

# Stage everything that has changed
git add .
```

**Important notes**

- `git add .` adds **all** changes in the current directory *and* its sub‑directories.  
- If a file is new, `git add` tells Git to start tracking it.  
- If a file is already tracked, `git add` simply records the new content.

### 1.2 Adding by Pattern  

You can stage files that match a pattern, which is handy for bulk actions:

```bash
# Stage all Python files
git add *.py

# Stage everything except Markdown files
git add -- ':!*.md'
```

The `--` separates options from the pathspec, preventing accidental interpretation of a filename as an option.

### 1.3 Removing Files from the Staging Area  

Sometimes you add too much. Use `git reset` (without arguments) to **unstage**:

```bash
# Unstage a single file
git reset README.md

# Unstage everything (keep the changes in the working tree)
git reset
```

> **Tip:** `git status` is your best friend. It shows three columns: *Untracked*, *Changes not staged for commit*, and *Changes to be committed*. Use it often to see what’s staged.

### 1.4 A Quick Staging Workflow Example  

```bash
# 1️⃣ Edit files
nano README.md          # fix typo
vim config.py           # add FEATURE_FLAG

# 2️⃣ Check what changed
git status

# 3️⃣ Stage only the README fix
git add README.md

# 4️⃣ Verify staging
git status
```

At this point, `README.md` is ready for a commit, while `config.py` remains only in your working directory.

---

## 2. Creating Commits – Capturing a Snapshot with Meaning  

A **commit** is a permanent snapshot of the staged files, plus a message that explains *why* the snapshot exists. Commits form the linear backbone of your project’s history.

### 2.1 The Basic Commit Command  

```bash
git commit -m "Fix typo in README and add brief usage example"
```

* `-m` supplies the commit message directly on the command line.  
* The message should be concise yet informative—think of it as a headline for future readers.

### 2.2 Writing Good Commit Messages  

A well‑crafted message makes the history readable for you and anyone else who later works on the project.

**Structure (recommended for beginners):**

```
<type>(<scope>): <short summary>

<optional longer description>

<footer>
```

* **type** – what kind of change? (`feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`)  
* **scope** – the part of the codebase affected (`README`, `config`, `parser`)  
* **short summary** – ≤50 characters, imperative mood (`Add`, `Fix`, `Update`)  
* **longer description** – optional, explains *how* and *why* the change was made.  
* **footer** – optional, e.g., “Closes #42” to link to an issue tracker.

**Example**

```
fix(README): correct spelling error

The word “environment” was misspelled as “enviroment”. This
fixes the typo and adds a short example of how to run the
script.

Closes #7
```

Even if you don’t adopt the full format right away, the key is to be **clear** and **specific**.

### 2.3 Common Commit Flags  

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `-a` | Automatically stage *all* tracked files before committing (skip `git add`). |
| `--amend` | Replace the most recent commit with a new one (useful for fixing a bad message or missed files). |
| `-v` | Show the diff of staged changes in the editor when writing a commit message. |
| `--no-edit` | When amending, keep the existing message unchanged. |

**Example – Amending a Commit**

Suppose you committed but forgot to add `config.py`:

```bash
git add config.py
git commit --amend -m "Fix typo in README and add FEATURE_FLAG"
```

Now the new commit contains both the README fix **and** the config change.

### 2.4 Atomic Commits – One Idea per Commit  

An *atomic* commit captures a single logical change. This makes later navigation, debugging, and collaboration much easier.

**Scenario**

You are polishing the documentation and also refactoring a function. Instead of bundling both into one commit, split them:

```bash
# 1️⃣ Stage and commit the documentation changes
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: clarify installation steps"

# 2️⃣ Stage and commit the code refactor
git add parser.py
git commit -m "refactor(parser): simplify token parsing"
```

Each commit now tells a clear story, and tools like `git bisect` can pinpoint the exact change that introduced a bug.

---

## 3. Reading the Commit History – Exploring the Timeline  

Once you have a series of commits, you’ll often need to look back: “When did we introduce the feature flag?” or “What was the last change before the bug appeared?”

### 3.1 The Basic `git log`  

Running `git log` prints the commit history in reverse chronological order.

```bash
git log
```

Typical output includes:

```
commit 9f2c3e7a4b1d2e8f9a4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f4a
Author: Alice <alice@example.com>
Date:   Tue Jul 23 14:32:10 2024 -0400

    fix(README): correct spelling error
```

### 3.2 Formatting Options  

You rarely need the full default view. Git provides many flags to tailor the output to your needs.

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `--oneline` | Shows each commit on a single line (`<hash> <message>`). |
| `--graph` | Draws an ASCII graph of branches and merges (useful when you later learn branching). |
| `--decorate` | Adds symbolic names like `HEAD`, `master`, or tags. |
| `--pretty=format:"%h %ad %s"` | Custom format; `%h` = short hash, `%ad` = author date, `%s` = subject. |
| `--stat` | Shows a summary of files changed and insertions/deletions. |
| `-n <num>` or `--max-count=<num>` | Limits the output to the most recent *n* commits. |
| `--since="2 weeks ago"` | Shows commits newer than the given date. |
| `--author="Alice"` | Filters commits by author name. |
| `--grep="feature"` | Shows only commits whose message contains the word “feature”. |

**Example – A Compact, Colored One‑Liner**

```bash
git log --oneline --decorate --color
```

Result (sample):

```
9f2c3e7 (HEAD -> master) fix(README): correct spelling error
a1b2c3d docs: add usage example to README
5e6f7a8 feat(config): introduce FEATURE_FLAG
```

### 3.3 Searching the History  

You can combine flags to locate a particular change:

```bash
# Find the commit that introduced FEATURE_FLAG
git log --grep="FEATURE_FLAG" --author="Alice" -n 1
```

Or, to see only commits from the last three days:

```bash
git log --since="3 days ago" --oneline
```

### 3.4 Visualizing History with `git log --graph`  

Even before you learn branching, the graph view can help you see the linear flow:

```bash
git log --graph --oneline --decorate
```

Sample output:

```
* 9f2c3e7 (HEAD -> master) fix(README): correct spelling error
* a1b2c3d docs: add usage example to README
* 5e6f7a8 feat(config): introduce FEATURE_FLAG
```

The asterisk (`*`) shows each commit; arrows would appear once you have multiple branches.

---

## 4. Comparing Changes – `git diff` in Action  

While `git log` tells you **what** happened, `git diff` tells you **how** the files changed.

### 4.1 Types of Diffs  

| Situation | Command | What it compares |
|-----------|---------|------------------|
| Working tree vs. staging area | `git diff` | Unstaged changes |
| Staging area vs. last commit (`HEAD`) | `git diff --cached` (or `--staged`) | Staged changes ready to commit |
| Two arbitrary commits | `git diff <commitA> <commitB>` | Changes between two snapshots |
| Specific file across commits | `git diff <commitA> <commitB> -- path/to/file` | Diff for one file only |

### 4.2 Basic Diff Output  

Running `git diff` after editing `README.md` but before staging shows a familiar “unified” format:

```
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index e69de29..4b825dc 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-# My Project
+# My Awesome Project
```

Lines prefixed with `-` were removed; lines with `+` were added.

### 4.3 Diff Options for Better Readability  

* `--color` – Color‑highlights additions (green) and deletions (red).  
* `--stat` – Shows a summary of how many files changed, insertions, and deletions.  
* `-p` – Shows the full patch (default for `git diff`).  
* `--name-only` – Lists only the filenames that changed.  

**Example – Quick Overview of Staged Changes**

```bash
git diff --cached --stat
```

Sample output:

```
 README.md | 2 +-
 config.py | 5 ++---
 2 files changed, 3 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

### 4.4 Real‑World Comparison Scenarios  

#### Scenario 1 – Verify What You’re About to Commit  

```bash
# Stage the README fix
git add README.md

# Inspect staged changes before committing
git diff --cached
```

If the diff looks correct, you can safely commit.

#### Scenario 2 – Find the Exact Change That Introduced a Bug  

Suppose a test started failing after a recent commit. You can diff the last two commits:

```bash
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD -- tests/test_feature.py
```

If the diff shows an unintended change, you now know where to start debugging.

#### Scenario 3 – Review a Pull Request Locally (pre‑remote)  

Even before pushing to a remote server, you can compare your work against a target branch (e.g., `main`):

```bash
git diff main..feature-branch --stat
```

This shows exactly what the feature branch would add to `main`.

---

## 5. Putting It All Together – A Mini Workflow  

Below is a concise, end‑to‑end example that demonstrates the three core actions in a realistic development loop.

```bash
# 1️⃣ Create a fresh repository (skip if you already have one)
mkdir demo && cd demo
git init

# 2️⃣ Add an initial file
echo "# Demo Project" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: bootstrap README"

# 3️⃣ Make a change – fix a typo
sed -i 's/Demo/Example/' README.md

# 4️⃣ See what changed
git status          # shows README.md as modified
git diff            # shows the actual diff (unstaged)

# 5️⃣ Stage the change
git add README.md

# 6️⃣ Verify staged diff
git diff --cached

# 7️⃣ Commit with a clear message
git commit -m "docs: replace ‘Demo’ with ‘Example’ in README"

# 8️⃣ Look at the history in a compact form
git log --oneline --decorate

# 9️⃣ Add a new feature flag
echo "FEATURE_FLAG = True" >> config.py

# 10️⃣ Stage and commit in one step (using -a)
git commit -am "feat(config): introduce FEATURE_FLAG"

# 11️⃣ Review the last two commits
git log -2 --pretty=format:"%h %s"
```

Running through this sequence gives you a clean history, each commit reflecting a single logical change, and the ability to glance at the diff whenever you need reassurance.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Staging (`git add`)** puts selected changes into the index, the *holding pen* for the next commit. Use `git status` frequently to see what’s staged versus what’s still in your working tree.  
- **Committing (`git commit`)** creates a permanent snapshot with a **descriptive message**. Good messages are short, imperative, and explain *why* the change matters.  
- **Viewing history (`git log`)** lets you navigate the timeline of snapshots. Flags like `--oneline`, `--graph`, and `--pretty` tailor the output for quick scanning or deeper investigation.  
- **Comparing (`git diff`)** shows the exact line‑by‑line changes between any two states: working tree ↔ index, index ↔ last commit, or any two commits. Options such as `--stat` and `--name-only` give high‑level overviews.  
- **Atomic commits**—one idea per commit—make the history easier to read, debug, and collaborate on.  
- A typical workflow: edit → `git status` → `git add` → `git diff --cached` (optional) → `git commit -m "type(scope): short summary"` → `git log` (as needed).  

Mastering these actions equips you with the ability to **save**, **track**, and **understand** every step of your project’s evolution, laying a solid foundation for the more advanced topics that follow.

modules.title: Branching Basics: Creating, Switching, Merging
