## A Real‑World “What‑If” Imagine you are working on a small web app that currently shows a static homepage. A product manager asks for a **new “Contact Us” page** that can be developed and tested without disturbing the live homepage. How can you start building the new page, keep the existing code safe, and later bring the finished work back into the main line of development? The answer is **branching** – creating a parallel line of development that you can switch to, work on, and later merge back. In this chapter you’ll learn how to create branches, hop between them, combine their histories, and tidy up after a successful merge. --- ## Creating Branches A *branch* is simply a pointer to a commit. The default branch created by Git is usually called **`main`** (or `master` in older repositories). Adding a new branch gives you a fresh place to commit changes while the original line stays untouched. ### The Basic Command ```bash git branch ``` - **`git branch`** lists existing branches when run without arguments. - Adding a name creates a new branch that starts at the **current commit** (the one you are on right now). > **Tip:** Branches are lightweight – they are just references, not copies of files. Changing one branch does not affect another until you merge. ### Example 1 – Starting a “Contact” Feature ```bash # You are on main, with the latest homepage code committed git branch contact-page # creates a new branch called contact-page git branch # shows: * main contact-page ``` At this point both `main` and `contact-page` point to the same commit. The asterisk (`*`) indicates the branch you are currently *checked out* (more on that soon). ### Naming Conventions Consistent names make it easier for you and teammates to understand the purpose of a branch: | Pattern | Meaning | |---------|---------| | `feature/` | New functionality (e.g., `feature/contact-page`) | | `bugfix/` | Fix for a specific bug (e.g., `bugfix/123`) | | `hotfix/` | Urgent fix on production code | | `experiment/` | Throw‑away work that may be discarded | You can use any name you like, but the above conventions are common in many teams. --- ## Switching Between Branches Creating a branch does not automatically move you to it. To start editing on the new line you must **check out** (or **switch**) to that branch. ### `git checkout` – The Classic Way ```bash git checkout ``` - Updates the working directory to match the commit the branch points to. - Moves the HEAD pointer (the symbolic name for “the current commit”) to the chosen branch. ### `git switch` – A Safer, Simpler Alias Git 2.23 introduced `git switch` to make the intent clearer: ```bash git switch ``` - Works exactly like `git checkout` for branch changes, but it does **not** handle file‑level operations (e.g., `git checkout `), reducing accidental misuse. Both commands will: 1. Update the files in your working tree to reflect the chosen branch’s snapshot. 2. Record the new branch as the current one (the asterisk moves). ### Example 2 – Jumping to the Feature Branch ```bash git switch contact-page # or: git checkout contact-page # Now the prompt shows: (contact-page) ``` You can verify where you are with: ```bash git status # shows "On branch contact-page" ``` ### Switching Back When you’re done with the feature work and want to see the stable homepage again: ```bash git switch main # returns to the main branch ``` All changes you made while on `contact-page` remain recorded in that branch’s history, invisible to `main` until you decide to merge. --- ## Merging Branches Once the “Contact Us” page is ready and tested, you want to **integrate** those changes back into `main`. That process is called **merging**. ### Fast‑Forward vs. Three‑Way Merge Git decides how to merge based on the relationship between the two branches: | Situation | Result | |-----------|--------| | **Fast‑forward** – `main` has not moved since the branch was created. The branch is simply *ahead* of `main`. | Git moves the `main` pointer forward to the branch tip – no extra commit is created. | | **Three‑way** – Both `main` and the branch have new commits. | Git creates a new *merge commit* that has two parents, representing the combined histories. | ### Performing a Merge ```bash git switch main # ensure you are on the branch that will receive the changes git merge ``` - If a fast‑forward is possible, Git will silently move `main`. - If a three‑way merge is needed, Git will open your default editor to let you edit the merge commit message. ### Example 3 – Merging the Contact Feature Assume you have added the contact page, committed the changes, and now want to bring them into `main`. ```bash # 1. Verify you are on main git switch main # 2. Merge the feature branch git merge contact-page ``` If `main` had no new commits after you created `contact-page`, the merge will be a fast‑forward: ``` Updating abc123..def456 Fast-forward ``` If `main` had received a small typo fix in the meantime, Git will create a merge commit: ``` Merge made by the 'recursive' strategy. contact.html | 12 ++++++------ 1 file changed, 6 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-) ``` ### Simple Conflict Resolution A **conflict** occurs when the same part of a file was edited differently on the two branches. Git will pause the merge and mark the conflicted files. ```bash git merge contact-page # ...output shows conflict in contact.html... ``` Open the conflicted file; Git inserts markers: ```html <<<<<<< HEAD

Contact us at info@example.com

=======

Reach us: contact@example.com

>>>>>>> contact-page ``` - The code between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is the version from the current branch (`main`). - The code between `=======` and `>>>>>>> contact-page` is from the branch being merged. **Resolve** by editing the file to the desired final state, then: ```bash git add contact.html # mark as resolved git commit # completes the merge ``` Because the conflict was simple (just a single line), the resolution is straightforward, but the same steps apply to any conflict. --- ## Deleting Branches After a Successful Merge Once a branch’s work is safely incorporated into another branch, the branch itself becomes unnecessary clutter. Git lets you delete it locally. ### Safe Deletion – `-d` ```bash git branch -d ``` - Git checks that the branch’s tip is reachable from the current branch (i.e., it has been merged). - If the branch is *not* merged, Git aborts and warns you. ### Force Deletion – `-D` ```bash git branch -D ``` - Skips the safety check and deletes the branch regardless of its merge status. - Use with caution; you may lose work that isn’t reachable from any other branch. ### Example 4 – Cleaning Up ```bash git switch main # ensure you are on the branch that contains the merged work git branch -d contact-page # safe delete; succeeds because it was merged git branch -v # shows only * main remains ``` If you had tried to delete a branch that still contained unmerged commits, Git would have printed: ``` error: The branch 'contact-page' is not fully merged. ``` You could then either merge it first or force‑delete with `-D` if you are sure the work is no longer needed. --- ## End‑to‑End Walkthrough Below is a compact script that demonstrates the whole lifecycle – from branch creation to deletion – using the “Contact Us” feature scenario. ```bash # 1. Start on main (already created and committed) git status # On branch main # 2. Create a new feature branch git branch feature/contact-page git switch feature/contact-page # 3. Add the new page (simulated) echo "

Contact Us

" > contact.html git add contact.html git commit -m "Add skeleton for Contact page" # 4. Switch back to main to continue other work git switch main # (optional) make a tiny typo fix on main echo "" >> index.html git add index.html git commit -m "Fix typo in homepage" # 5. Merge the feature branch git merge feature/contact-page # creates a merge commit because both sides changed # 6. Resolve a conflict (if any) # (Assume conflict occurred, edit contact.html, then:) git add contact.html git commit # finishes merge # 7. Delete the feature branch git branch -d feature/contact-page ``` Running the script step‑by‑step in a fresh repository will let you see each command’s effect, reinforcing the concepts introduced in this chapter. --- ## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet - **Create a branch** – `git branch ` - **List branches** – `git branch` (no arguments) - **Switch to a branch** – `git switch ` *or* `git checkout ` - **Merge a branch into the current one** – `git merge ` - **Resolve a conflict** – edit file → `git add ` → `git commit` - **Delete a merged branch** – `git branch -d ` - **Force‑delete** – `git branch -D ` --- ## Key Takeaways - A **branch** gives you an isolated line of development; creating one is as easy as `git branch `. - Use **`git switch`** (or the classic `git checkout`) to move your working directory onto the branch you want to edit. - **Merging** integrates changes; Git will fast‑forward when possible or create a merge commit otherwise. - Simple conflicts appear as markers inside the affected files; resolve them, stage the file, and commit to finish the merge. - After a successful merge, clean up with `git branch -d `; only use `-D` when you are certain the branch’s work is no longer needed. With these tools you can safely experiment, develop new features in parallel, and keep your main codebase stable—foundations that will serve you well as you move on to remote collaboration and more advanced workflows.

modules.title: Working with Remote Repositories
modules.content:
## Why Work with Remotes?

Imagine you have just finished a small script on your laptop. You want to keep a copy safe **and** share it with a teammate who works from a different city. Storing the code only on your machine means:

* If your laptop crashes, the work disappears.  
* Your teammate cannot see or edit the code without you sending files manually.

A **remote repository** solves both problems. It lives on a server (GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab, etc.) that multiple developers can reach over the internet. Your local copy talks to that server, sending (“pushing”) your changes and receiving (“pulling”) others’ work. From this point forward, “remote” always means *a repository that lives somewhere else* and is accessed via a URL.

---

## Cloning a Repository

The first step in using a remote is to **clone** it. Cloning creates a brand‑new local repository that is already linked to the remote and copies all existing commits.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/username/project.git
```

* `git clone` – the command that does the work.  
* The URL – tells Git *where* the remote lives. It can be an HTTPS link, an SSH link (`git@github.com:username/project.git`), or a read‑only URL for public repos.

When the command finishes, you have:

1. A directory named `project` containing the files.  
2. A hidden `.git` folder that tracks history.  
3. A default remote called **origin** that points to the URL you supplied.

> **Tip:** If you already have a local repository and want to add a remote later, skip cloning and use `git remote add` (see the next section).

---

## Understanding Remotes (`git remote`)

A remote is just a **named shortcut** to a URL. The default name **origin** is conventional, but you can add any number of additional remotes (e.g., `upstream`, `team‑repo`) to work with multiple servers.

### Adding and Listing Remotes

```bash
# Add a new remote named "upstream"
git remote add upstream https://github.com/organization/project.git

# Show all configured remotes
git remote -v
```

The `-v` flag displays both **fetch** and **push** URLs:

```
origin    https://github.com/username/project.git (fetch)
origin    https://github.com/username/project.git (push)
upstream  https://github.com/organization/project.git (fetch)
upstream  https://github.com/organization/project.git (push)
```

* **fetch URL** – where Git pulls changes from.  
* **push URL** – where Git sends your commits.  
Often the two are the same, but they can differ (e.g., read‑only fetch URL and a separate write‑access push URL).

You can rename or remove a remote with:

```bash
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote remove upstream
```

---

## Pushing Your Commits

After you have **committed** locally (see Chapter 4), you can share those commits with the remote using `git push`.

```bash
git push origin main
```

* `origin` – the remote name.  
* `main` – the branch you are sending.  

If the remote already has commits that you don’t have locally, Git will refuse the push and ask you to integrate those changes first (see the *pull* section). This safety net prevents accidentally overwriting someone else’s work.

### Pushing a New Branch

When you create a branch that doesn’t exist on the remote, you must tell Git to create it there:

```bash
git push -u origin feature‑login
```

* `-u` (or `--set-upstream`) records that `feature‑login` on `origin` is the default upstream for the local branch. After this, a simple `git push` (or `git pull`) will automatically target the correct remote branch.

---

## Pulling Updates

Fetching the latest changes from the remote and merging them into your current branch is done with `git pull`.

```bash
git pull origin main
```

Under the hood, `git pull` does two things:

1. **fetch** – download new commits from the remote.  
2. **merge** – integrate those commits into the current branch.

### Fast‑Forward vs. Merge Scenarios

* **Fast‑forward** – Your local branch is behind but has no divergent work. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward, resulting in a linear history.

  ```
  A---B---C   (origin/main)
          \
           D   (local/main)
  ```

  After `git pull`, the diagram becomes:

  ```
  A---B---C---D   (both branches)
  ```

* **Merge** – Both the remote and your local branch have new commits. Git creates a new **merge commit** that ties the two histories together.

  ```
  A---B---C   (origin/main)
   \       \
    D---E   (local/main)
  ```

  After `git pull`, you see a new commit `M`:

  ```
  A---B---C---M
   \       /
    D---E
  ```

  The merge commit records that you consciously combined two lines of development.

> **Why it matters:** Fast‑forward keeps the history tidy, while merge commits preserve the fact that two independent streams of work were combined. Some teams prefer one style over the other; the mechanics are the same.

If you prefer a fast‑forward‑only history, you can ask Git to refuse merges:

```bash
git pull --ff-only origin main
```

Git will abort with an error if a merge would be required, forcing you to resolve the situation manually (e.g., by rebasing).

---

## Fetching Without Merging

Sometimes you only want to **inspect** what others have pushed without altering your current work. `git fetch` does exactly that.

```bash
git fetch origin
```

After fetching, the remote’s branches appear under the namespace `origin/`. For example, `origin/main` reflects the latest state of the remote’s `main` branch, while your local `main` remains unchanged.

You can then compare the two:

```bash
git log --oneline ..origin/main   # commits you don’t have yet
git diff main..origin/main        # file differences
```

When you’re ready to incorporate the changes, you can merge or rebase manually:

```bash
git merge origin/main   # fast‑forward or merge
# or
git rebase origin/main  # replay your work on top of the remote
```

Fetching is especially handy when you:

* Want to see if a teammate’s feature branch is ready for review.  
* Need to resolve a complex merge conflict but prefer to work on a clean copy first.  
* Are on a low‑bandwidth connection and wish to avoid the overhead of an automatic merge.

---

## Practical Example 1: Solo Project on GitHub

**Scenario:** You are writing a command‑line tool on your laptop and want a backup on GitHub.

1. **Create a remote repository** on GitHub (click *New repository*, give it a name, leave it empty).  
2. **Initialize locally** (Chapter 3) and make a first commit:

   ```bash
   git init
   echo "# MyTool" > README.md
   git add README.md
   git commit -m "Initial commit"
   ```

3. **Add the remote** (you could also have cloned an empty repo, but this shows the add approach):

   ```bash
   git remote add origin https://github.com/youruser/mytool.git
   ```

4. **Push the first commit**:

   ```bash
   git push -u origin main
   ```

   The `-u` flag records that `main` on `origin` is the upstream for your local `main`.

5. **Later, after adding a feature**, you commit locally and push again:

   ```bash
   git add feature.py
   git commit -m "Add login feature"
   git push
   ```

   Because the upstream is already set, the simple `git push` knows where to send the new commit.

Now your code is safely stored on GitHub and can be cloned on any other machine with `git clone`.

---

## Practical Example 2: Team Collaboration on Bitbucket

**Scenario:** A small team of three developers works on a web app stored on Bitbucket. Each developer clones the same repo, creates a feature branch, and pushes their work.

1. **Clone the shared repository** (once per developer):

   ```bash
   git clone https://bitbucket.org/team/webapp.git
   cd webapp
   ```

2. **Create a feature branch**:

   ```bash
   git checkout -b feature-search
   # edit files …
   git add .
   git commit -m "Implement search UI"
   ```

3. **Push the branch** so teammates can see it:

   ```bash
   git push -u origin feature-search
   ```

4. **Pulling teammates’ updates**: Suppose a teammate added a bug‑fix on `main`. Before merging your feature, you bring the latest `main` into your branch.

   ```bash
   git checkout main
   git pull                 # fast‑forward if possible
   git checkout feature-search
   git merge main           # creates a merge commit if needed
   ```

5. **Fetching without merging**: While reviewing a teammate’s new branch `feature-api`, you just want to glance at the changes:

   ```bash
   git fetch origin
   git diff origin/feature-api   # shows differences against your current branch
   ```

   If the diff looks good, you can later merge it:

   ```bash
   git checkout main
   git merge origin/feature-api
   ```

This workflow demonstrates the typical cycle of **clone → branch → commit → push → fetch/pull → merge** that underpins most collaborative Git projects.

---

## Common Pitfalls and Tips

| Issue | Why it Happens | Quick Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----------|
| **“rejected” push** (`! [rejected]`) | Remote has commits you don’t have locally. | `git pull --rebase` then `git push`. |
| **Accidentally pushing to the wrong remote** | Multiple remotes (e.g., `origin` and `backup`). | Use `git remote -v` to verify, then `git push <correct‑remote> <branch>`. |
| **Merge conflicts after a pull** | Both you and someone else edited the same lines. | Resolve conflicts in the editor, `git add` the resolved files, then `git commit`. |
| **Forgot to set upstream** | `git push` says “no upstream branch”. | Run `git push -u origin <branch>` once; thereafter plain `git push` works. |
| **Large files slowing down fetch/pull** | Binary assets (images, compiled libraries) are not ideal for Git. | Store them in a separate artifact store or use Git LFS. |

**Additional tips for beginners**

* **Use HTTPS for the first few weeks** – you only need to type your username/password (or a personal access token) and avoid the extra SSH‑key setup.  
* **Commit often, push often** – small, frequent pushes make merges easier and keep the remote a reliable backup.  
* **Read the remote’s documentation** – GitHub, Bitbucket, and GitLab have slightly different default branch names (`main` vs. `master`) and UI features.  
* **Keep your remote URLs tidy** – naming conventions like `origin` for your personal fork and `upstream` for the main project help avoid confusion.

---

## Key Takeaways

* A **remote repository** lives on a server and lets you share and back up your work.  
* `git clone <url>` creates a local copy that is already linked to the remote (named **origin** by default).  
* `git remote` lets you **add**, **list**, **rename**, or **remove** named shortcuts to remote URLs.  
* **Pushing** (`git push`) sends your local commits to a remote branch; use `-u` to set the upstream for future pushes.  
* **Pulling** (`git pull`) fetches new commits and merges them; understand the difference between **fast‑forward** (linear) and **merge** (creates a merge commit).  
* **Fetching** (`git fetch`) downloads remote changes without altering your current branch, giving you a safe way to inspect others’ work.  
* Common errors—rejected pushes, missing upstreams, merge conflicts—are resolved by pulling (or rebasing) first, setting upstreams, and manually fixing conflicts.  

Mastering these commands turns a solitary local repository into a collaborative hub, laying the groundwork for the more advanced workflows (forks, pull requests) covered in later chapters. Happy coding!

modules.title: Collaboration Workflow: Forks and Pull Requests
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Story: Fixing a Typo in an Open‑Source Library  

You are reading the documentation for a popular JavaScript library when you spot a typo that could confuse new users. You decide to **contribute a fix**. Because you do not have write access to the library’s main repository, you will use the *fork‑and‑pull‑request* workflow that powers most open‑source projects. By the end of this chapter you will have walked through every step of that workflow: forking a repository, cloning it locally, keeping it in sync with the original project, creating a dedicated branch for your fix, pushing the change to your fork, and finally opening a pull request (PR) that the maintainers can review and merge.

---

## What Is a Fork and Why Do We Need It?  

A **fork** is a personal copy of a repository that lives on a hosting service such as GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Unlike the *clone* you performed in earlier chapters (which creates a local copy on your computer), a fork lives on the remote server and is owned by *you* rather than the original project.  

- **Purpose** – The fork gives you a sandbox where you can push commits without affecting the upstream project.  
- **Ownership** – The remote you cloned from in “Working with Remote Repositories” is called **origin**; after forking, **origin** points to *your* fork, while the original project becomes the **upstream** remote.  

Think of a fork as a personal workspace that you can freely experiment in, while still being able to propose changes back to the original project.

> **Note:** Some organizations grant direct write access to collaborators. In that case you would skip the fork step and work directly on a branch in the shared repository. This chapter focuses on the *public* open‑source model where most contributors start with a fork.

---

## Step 1 – Fork the Repository on the Hosting Platform  

1. **Navigate to the upstream repository** (e.g., `https://github.com/example/markdown‑parser`).  
2. Click the **Fork** button (usually in the top‑right corner).  
3. Choose your personal account or an organization you belong to.  

The platform creates a new repository under your account, e.g., `https://github.com/your‑username/markdown‑parser`. This is now your *fork* and will serve as the remote called **origin** when you clone it.

> **Tip:** The forked repository starts as an exact replica of the upstream project, including all branches, tags, and commit history.

---

## Step 2 – Clone Your Fork Locally and Set the Upstream Remote  

### 2.1 Clone the Fork  

Open a terminal and run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-username/markdown-parser.git
cd markdown-parser
```

This creates a local directory containing the full history of the project, exactly as described in “Creating and Inspecting Local Repositories”.

### 2.2 Verify the Default Remote  

```bash
git remote -v
```

You will see something like:

```
origin  https://github.com/your-username/markdown-parser.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/your-username/markdown-parser.git (push)
```

At this point **origin** points to *your* fork.

### 2.3 Add the Upstream Remote  

```bash
git remote add upstream https://github.com/example/markdown-parser.git
```

Now you have two remotes:

- **origin** – your personal fork (read/write)
- **upstream** – the original project (read‑only for you)

Run `git remote -v` again to confirm:

```
origin    https://github.com/your-username/markdown-parser.git (fetch)
origin    https://github.com/your-username/markdown-parser.git (push)
upstream  https://github.com/example/markdown-parser.git (fetch)
upstream  https://github.com/example/markdown-parser.git (push)
```

> **Why keep an upstream remote?**  
> It lets you pull in the latest changes from the original project, ensuring your fork does not drift apart. This is especially important when the upstream repository is active.

---

## Step 3 – Create a Feature Branch  

Working directly on the default `main` (or `master`) branch is discouraged because it mixes your work with the upstream’s stable code. Instead, create a **feature branch** that isolates your change.

```bash
# Make sure you are up‑to‑date with upstream's main branch
git fetch upstream
git checkout -b main upstream/main   # creates a local copy of upstream's main
git pull upstream main                # ensure it is current

# Now create a descriptive branch for the typo fix
git checkout -b typo/fix‑readme
```

The branch name `typo/fix‑readme` follows the convention `type/short‑description`, making it clear what the branch contains.  

> **Tip:** Branch names should be short, lower‑case, and use hyphens (`-`) or slashes (`/`) as separators. Avoid spaces.

---

## Step 4 – Make Changes, Commit, and Push  

### 4.1 Edit the File  

Open the file that contains the typo, e.g., `README.md`, using your favorite editor and correct the mistake.

### 4.2 Stage and Commit  

```bash
git add README.md
git commit -m "Fix typo: 'instal' → 'install' in README"
```

The commit message follows the guidance from “Committing Changes and Viewing History”: start with a concise summary, optionally followed by a blank line and a longer description if needed.

### 4.3 Push the Branch to Your Fork  

```bash
git push -u origin typo/fix-readme
```

- The `-u` flag sets **origin/typo/fix‑readme** as the *upstream* tracking branch, so future `git pull` and `git push` commands can be issued without specifying the remote and branch name.  

You can verify the push on the hosting platform; the branch should now appear under the “Branches” tab of your fork.

---

## Step 5 – Open a Pull Request  

A **pull request** (sometimes called a *merge request*) is a web‑based request to merge your branch into another branch—usually the upstream’s `main`.  

1. Go to the page of your fork on GitHub.  
2. You will see a banner: *“Your recently pushed branches: typo/fix-readme – Compare & pull request”*. Click the **Compare & pull request** button.  
3. GitHub automatically sets the **base repository** to `example/markdown-parser` and the **base branch** to `main`. The **head repository** is your fork, and the **compare branch** is `typo/fix-readme`.  
4. Fill in the PR form:  
   - **Title:** `Fix typo in README`  
   - **Description:** Briefly explain why the change matters.  
   - Optionally add screenshots or links to related issues.  
5. Click **Create pull request**.

Your PR is now visible to the maintainers of the upstream project. They can review the changes, discuss them, and eventually merge them.

> **Pro tip:** If the upstream project uses a different branching model (e.g., `develop` instead of `main`), make sure you select the correct base branch when opening the PR.

---

## Step 6 – Responding to Review Comments  

Once the PR is open, reviewers may leave **review comments**. These can be simple suggestions, questions, or requests for changes. Here’s a typical workflow:

1. **Read the feedback** – comments appear inline (next to the relevant lines) and/or in the PR’s “Conversation” tab.  
2. **Make the requested changes** on the same feature branch. For example, a reviewer asks you to update the documentation link.  

```bash
# Edit the file again
git add README.md
git commit --amend   # modifies the most recent commit
# Or create a new commit if you prefer
git push
```

If you used `--amend`, you need to force‑push because you rewrote history:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease
```

3. **Mark the conversation as resolved** – on GitHub, click the “Resolve conversation” button after you push the fix.  

4. **Wait for re‑review** – the maintainer may approve the PR or ask for additional tweaks.  

When the PR finally receives an **Approved** review, a maintainer will merge it. After merging, you can clean up:

```bash
# Delete the remote branch
git push origin --delete typo/fix-readme
# Delete the local branch
git branch -d typo/fix-readme
```

### Real‑World Example 1: Contributing a New Feature  

You want to add a `markdown‑to‑HTML` conversion option to the same library. The steps are identical, except the feature branch might be named `feature/markdown-to-html`. After implementing the code, you open a PR, and reviewers ask you to add unit tests. You create a new commit with tests, push, and the reviewers approve.

### Real‑World Example 2: Updating Documentation for a Theme  

A popular static‑site theme has outdated instructions for installing a plugin. You fork the theme repository, create a branch `docs/update‑plugin‑install`, edit `docs/installation.md`, and open a PR. The maintainer suggests adding a code block with the exact command line. You edit, amend the commit, push, and the PR is merged.

### Real‑World Example 3: Fixing a Build Failure in a CLI Tool  

A continuous‑integration (CI) pipeline fails because a new version of a dependency introduces a breaking change. You fork the CLI tool repo, create a branch `bug/fix‑ci‑failure`, modify the `package.json` version constraint, and open a PR. Reviewers request you to also bump the changelog. You add the entry, push, and the PR passes all checks before being merged.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Fix / Prevention |
|---------|----------------|------------------|
| **Pushing directly to `main`** | Forgetting to create a feature branch or assuming you have permission. | Always start a new branch from `upstream/main` before making changes. |
| **Missing upstream sync** | Working on an outdated fork; merge conflicts arise later. | Periodically run `git fetch upstream && git merge upstream/main` (or `git rebase upstream/main`) on your local `main` branch. |
| **Forgetting to set the remote tracking branch** | Using `git push` without `-u` leads to ambiguous pushes later. | Use `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time you push a new branch. |
| **Force‑pushing without caution** | Overwrites history on the remote, potentially discarding teammates’ work. | Use `git push --force-with-lease` which aborts if the remote has advanced since you last fetched. |
| **Leaving review comments unresolved** | The PR appears unfinished, delaying merge. | After each push, click “Resolve conversation” for the relevant comments. |

---

## Keeping Your Fork Fresh (Optional but Recommended)

Even after a PR is merged, you may want to continue contributing. To keep your fork from diverging:

```bash
# From the local main branch
git checkout main
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main   # or git rebase upstream/main
git push origin main
```

Now your fork’s `main` branch mirrors the upstream `main`. Future feature branches will start from a clean, up‑to‑date base.

---

## Summary of Commands  

| Action | Command |
|--------|---------|
| Fork on platform | *(click UI button)* |
| Clone fork | `git clone <fork‑url>` |
| Add upstream remote | `git remote add upstream <upstream‑url>` |
| Fetch upstream updates | `git fetch upstream` |
| Create feature branch | `git checkout -b <branch‑name>` |
| Stage changes | `git add <files>` |
| Commit | `git commit -m "Message"` |
| Push branch | `git push -u origin <branch‑name>` |
| Open PR | *(via web UI)* |
| Amend last commit | `git commit --amend` |
| Force‑push after amend | `git push --force-with-lease` |
| Delete remote branch after merge | `git push origin --delete <branch‑name>` |
| Clean up local branch | `git branch -d <branch‑name>` |

---

## ## Key Takeaways  

- **Fork** creates a personal remote copy of a project; **clone** brings that copy onto your local machine.  
- After cloning your fork, **add an upstream remote** pointing to the original repository so you can stay synchronized.  
- Always **create a dedicated feature branch** for each logical change; never commit directly to `main`.  
- **Commit** your changes with a clear message, then **push** the branch to your fork (`origin`).  
- Open a **pull request** from your feature branch to the upstream’s target branch; this is the formal way to propose changes.  
- Reviewers may ask for adjustments; you can **amend** or add commits, **push** (often with `--force-with-lease`), and **resolve** comments.  
- Once the PR is merged, clean up both remote and local branches, and **keep your fork up‑to‑date** by regularly pulling from upstream.  

By mastering this fork‑and‑pull‑request workflow, you can confidently contribute to any open‑source project, collaborate with maintainers, and become an active member of the global software community.

modules.content:
## The Moment You Hit “Oops”

You’ve been working on a new feature for a few hours. You added a handful of files, edited several others, and finally ran:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add experimental widget"
```

You push the branch, open a pull request, and—*boom*—your teammate spots a typo in a comment that you never intended to ship. Or perhaps you realize that the last commit introduced a bug, and you need to roll it back before anyone else builds on top of it.  

These situations are common, and Git gives you three distinct tool‑sets for handling them safely:

* **`git checkout -- <path>`** – discard *unstaged* changes.
* **`git revert <commit>`** – create a new commit that undoes a previous one.
* **`git reset`** – move the HEAD pointer and optionally rewrite the index and working tree.

Below we’ll explore each command, when to use it, and how to combine them with **`git reflog`** to rescue a commit you thought was lost.

---

## 1. Undoing Unstaged Changes with `git checkout --`

### 1.1 What “unstaged” means

When you modify a file, the change lives only in your **working tree** until you tell Git to track it with `git add`. Those modifications are *unstaged*—they haven’t been recorded in the **index** (the staging area). If you haven’t added them yet, you can safely discard them.

### 1.2 The command

```bash
git checkout -- <pathspec>
```

* `<pathspec>` can be a single file, a directory, or `.` to mean “everything in the current directory and below”.
* The double‑dash (`--`) tells Git that everything that follows is a path, not a branch name.

### 1.3 Example: Reverting a Mistyped Variable

```bash
# You edit config.js and accidentally delete a line
$ git status
On branch feature/widget
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   config.js

# Discard the accidental edit
$ git checkout -- config.js
$ git status
On branch feature/widget
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

After the checkout, the file is exactly as it was in the last commit.

### 1.4 When *not* to use it

* If you have already staged the change (`git add`), `checkout --` will **not** affect the index. Use `git reset` (covered later) to unstage first.
* If you need to keep a copy of the change for later, consider stashing (`git stash`) instead of discarding.

---

## 2. Reverting a Commit with `git revert`

### 2.1 Why “revert” instead of “reset”?

`git reset` rewrites history by moving the branch tip backwards. That’s fine for private branches, but once a commit is **public** (pushed to a shared remote), rewriting history can break teammates’ clones. `git revert` solves the problem by *adding* a new commit that undoes the effects of an earlier one, preserving the linear history.

### 2.2 The command

```bash
git revert <commit>
```

* `<commit>` can be a SHA‑1 hash, a branch name, or any rev‑spec that resolves to a single commit.
* Git opens your default editor with a pre‑filled commit message like “Revert "Add experimental widget"”. Save and close to create the revert commit.

### 2.3 Example: Rolling Back a Broken Feature

Assume the following history (simplified):

```
A -- B -- C   (main)
```

*Commit C* introduced a bug. To undo it without rewriting history:

```bash
$ git revert C
# Editor opens:
# Revert "Add experimental widget"
#
# This reverts commit C2f4e5d.
#
# (Modify message if you like)

# After saving:
$ git log --oneline
D (HEAD -> main) Revert "Add experimental widget"
C Add experimental widget
B Refactor core API
A Initial commit
```

Now the repository contains a new commit **D** that neutralizes the changes introduced by **C**, while the original commit remains in history for audit purposes.

### 2.4 Reverting Multiple Commits

You can revert a range of commits in one go:

```bash
git revert --no-commit <oldest>^..<newest>
git commit -m "Revert a series of bad commits"
```

The `--no-commit` flag stages the inverse changes without creating intermediate commits, allowing you to bundle them into a single, tidy revert.

### 2.5 Edge Cases

* **Conflicts** – If the changes being reverted clash with later commits, Git will pause and ask you to resolve conflicts just like a normal merge. After fixing them, run `git revert --continue`.
* **Merge commits** – Reverting a merge requires `-m <parent-number>` to tell Git which side of the merge to treat as the mainline. This is an advanced use case; beginners can usually avoid it by reverting the individual commits that made up the merge.

---

## 3. Resetting the Index and Working Tree with `git reset`

`git reset` is the most flexible (and potentially dangerous) tool for undoing work. It moves the **HEAD** pointer to a specified commit and optionally updates the index and working tree.

### 3.1 The three reset modes

| Mode | Index | Working Tree | Typical Use |
|------|-------|--------------|-------------|
| `--soft` | **Yes** (keeps staged changes) | **No** (leaves them untouched) | Un‑commit recent changes while keeping them staged for amendment. |
| `--mixed` (default) | **Yes** (unstages) | **No** (leaves working files) | Undo a commit and move its changes back to the working tree. |
| `--hard` | **No** (clears index) | **No** (overwrites files) | Throw away all changes after a given commit – **use with caution**. |

### 3.2 Example 1: “I meant to amend”

You just committed, but you forgot to include a small fix.

```bash
# History: A -- B (HEAD)
# Want to edit B
$ git reset --soft HEAD~1   # Move HEAD back one commit, keep changes staged
$ git add missing_file.txt
$ git commit -m "Add experimental widget (updated)"
```

Now the repository has a single, corrected commit.

### 3.3 Example 2: “Undo the last commit, keep work”

```bash
# History: A -- B (HEAD)
$ git reset --mixed HEAD~1   # HEAD moves to A, index cleared, changes stay in working tree
$ git status
# On branch feature/widget
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified:   widget.js
#   new file:   helper.js
```

You can now edit, stage, or discard the changes as you wish.

### 3.4 Example 3: “Discard a broken experiment”

```bash
# History: A -- B -- C (HEAD)   # C is a messy experiment
$ git reset --hard B
```

All files revert to the state of commit **B**; the work introduced by **C** disappears from both the index and the working tree. The commit **C** still exists in the object database, but it becomes unreachable—*unless* you need it later, in which case `git reflog` can help (see next section).

### 3.5 Safety Tips

* **Never** run `git reset --hard` on a branch that others have pulled. It will rewrite history and cause downstream merges to fail.
* After a reset, run `git status` to confirm the state of your index and working tree.
* If you’re unsure, start with `--soft` or `--mixed`. You can always add `--hard` later once you’re confident.

---

## 4. Recovering Lost Commits with `git reflog`

Even the most careful developer can lose a commit—perhaps after a hard reset or an accidental checkout. Git maintains a **reference log** (`reflog`) that records where the HEAD and branch pointers have moved.

### 4.1 What the reflog shows

```bash
$ git reflog
b1e2f3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
a9c4d2e HEAD@{1}: commit: Add experimental widget
7f8e9a0 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to feature/widget
...
```

Each entry includes:

* The abbreviated commit SHA.
* A *relative* identifier (`HEAD@{n}`) you can use as a shortcut.
* A short description of the action that caused the move.

### 4.2 Restoring a lost commit

Suppose you performed a hard reset and later realized you need the discarded commit `a9c4d2e`.

```bash
# Find the SHA in the reflog (or use HEAD@{1})
$ git checkout a9c4d2e
# Create a new branch to preserve it
$ git checkout -b rescued-commit
```

Now the commit is reachable again, and you can merge or cherry‑pick it as needed.

### 4.3 Practical Workflow

1. **Accidentally reset** – Realize you lost changes.
2. **Run `git reflog`** – Locate the recent HEAD position.
3. **Create a branch** at that point (`git branch <temp> <sha>`).
4. **Cherry‑pick** or **merge** the recovered commit back onto your working branch.

### 4.4 How long does the reflog last?

By default, reflog entries expire after **90 days** (`git config --global gc.reflogExpire`). You can adjust this with `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` for commits that have become dangling.

---

## 5. Choosing the Right Tool for the Situation

| Situation | Recommended Command | Reason |
|-----------|---------------------|--------|
| **Discard local edits you haven’t staged** | `git checkout -- <file>` | Quick, no history impact. |
| **Undo a public commit that’s already pushed** | `git revert <commit>` | Creates a new, safe commit; history stays linear. |
| **Rewrite the last few local commits before sharing** | `git reset --soft` / `--mixed` | Keeps work but reshapes history; safe while still private. |
| **Completely discard a series of local commits** | `git reset --hard <good‑commit>` | Removes unwanted history; use only on private branches. |
| **Recover a commit you thought was lost** | `git reflog` + `git checkout` / `git branch` | Finds previous HEAD positions and restores them. |

---

## 6. Real‑World Walkthroughs

### 6.1 Scenario A: A Bad Pull Request Merge

Your team merges a pull request that unintentionally adds a large, debug‑only file. The merge is already on `origin/main`. You need to remove the file without rewriting the merge history.

```bash
# 1. Create a revert commit for the merge
git revert -m 1 <merge‑sha>

# 2. Push the revert
git push origin main
```

*`-m 1`* tells Git to treat the first parent (the pre‑merge branch) as the mainline, effectively undoing the merge’s changes while preserving the commit graph.

### 6.2 Scenario B: Accidentally Reset Hard on a Feature Branch

You’re experimenting on `feature/experiment`. After a failed build you run:

```bash
git reset --hard origin/feature/experiment
```

Later you realize you needed the work from the now‑lost commit `d4e5f6a`.  

```bash
# 1. Locate the commit in reflog
git reflog

# 2. Restore it on a new branch
git branch rescued d4e5f6a
git checkout rescued
# 3. Merge back if desired
git checkout feature/experiment
git merge rescued
```

Now the work is back, and the original branch remains clean.

### 6.3 Scenario C: Fixing a Small Mistake Before Pushing

You just committed a typo in `README.md` and haven’t pushed yet.

```bash
# 1. Un‑commit but keep changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# 2. Fix the typo
vim README.md

# 3. Amend the commit
git commit --amend -m "Update README with correct spelling"
```

No new commit is created; the history stays tidy, and the typo never leaves your local repository.

---

## 7. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

* **Running `checkout --` on a staged file** – The index remains unchanged, leading to a mismatch between staged and working versions. Use `git reset` first if you need to unstage.
* **Reverting a merge without `-m`** – Git will refuse, because it cannot guess which parent to treat as the mainline. Remember the `-m` flag for merge commits.
* **Hard resetting a shared branch** – This rewrites history that others may have based work on, causing “non‑fast‑forward” errors. Always coordinate with teammates or prefer `git revert`.
* **Forgetting to push after a revert** – The revert commit lives only locally until you push; teammates will continue to see the problematic changes.

---

## Key Takeaways

* **`git checkout -- <path>`** safely discards *unstaged* changes; it does not affect the index.
* **`git revert <commit>`** creates a new commit that undoes a previous one, preserving public history.
* **`git reset`** moves HEAD and can optionally rewrite the index and working tree:
  * `--soft` keeps staged changes,
  * `--mixed` unstages but keeps the work,
  * `--hard` throws everything away.
* **`git reflog`** records every movement of HEAD and branch pointers, enabling recovery of seemingly lost commits.
* Choose the command that matches the visibility of the commit:
  * Private/local → `reset` (rewriting history is safe).
  * Public/shared → `revert` (adds a safe “undo” commit).
* Always verify the state with `git status` and, when in doubt, work on a temporary branch before altering history.

# Best Practices for Effective Git Workflows

Imagine you’re working on a team project where multiple developers are making changes to the same codebase. One developer accidentally overwrites another’s work, another commits a password to the repository, and someone else merges a massive, untested branch that breaks the build. These are all common pitfalls in Git—and they’re all avoidable with the right practices.

This chapter will help you establish good habits, avoid common mistakes, and explore advanced Git techniques. By the end, you’ll know how to maintain a clean, efficient workflow and where to go for further learning.

## Adopting Commit Message Conventions

Clear, consistent commit messages make your Git history readable and maintainable. One widely adopted standard is **Conventional Commits**, which follows a structured format:

```
<type>(<scope>): <description>

<body>
<footer>
```

### Common Commit Types
- **feat**: A new feature
- **fix**: A bug fix
- **docs**: Documentation changes
- **style**: Code formatting (e.g., indentation)
- **refactor**: Code changes that neither fix bugs nor add features
- **test**: Adding or modifying tests
- **chore**: Maintenance tasks (e.g., dependency updates)

### Example Commit Messages
- `feat(api): add user authentication endpoint`
- `fix(login): prevent infinite redirect loop`
- `docs(readme): update installation instructions`

**Why it matters**: Well-structured commits help teams track changes efficiently. If you’re working on a project with others, check if they have a preferred convention.

## Keeping Branches Small and Merging Regularly

Branches are powerful tools for isolating work (as covered in *Branching Basics: Creating, Switching, Merging*), but they can become unwieldy if left unmanaged.

### Best Practices
- **Create small, focused branches** (e.g., `fix/login-error` instead of `update-everything`).
- **Merge or rebase frequently** to avoid long-lived branches that diverge from the main codebase.
- **Use descriptive branch names** (e.g., `feat/user-profile` instead of `branch1`).

### Real-World Example
A team working on a web app creates a branch called `feat/checkout-flow`. Instead of waiting months to merge it, they:
1. Break the work into smaller tasks (`feat/checkout-validation`, `feat/payment-integration`).
2. Merge each branch into `main` as soon as it’s tested.
3. Avoid a last-minute merge that could introduce conflicts.

## Avoiding Sensitive Data and Large Files

Git is not a secure place to store passwords, API keys, or large binary files (like videos or datasets).

### Risks of Committing Sensitive Data
- **Exposure**: Anyone with repository access can see the data.
- **Permanence**: Even if you delete the file later, it may remain in Git’s history.

### Solutions
- **Use `.gitignore`** to exclude sensitive files (e.g., `config.env`, `secrets.json`).
- **Store secrets in environment variables** or a secure vault (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager).
- **For large files**, use Git LFS (Large File Storage) or host them externally.

### Example Scenario
A developer commits a `config.js` file containing a database password. Even after deleting it, the password remains in Git history. The solution? Use `git filter-repo` to purge the file entirely from history.

## Exploring Advanced Git Techniques

Once you’re comfortable with the basics, you can explore more powerful Git features.

### Rebasing
- **What it does**: Rewrites commit history by moving or combining commits.
- **When to use**: Before merging a feature branch to keep history linear.
- **Example**:
  ```bash
  git checkout feature-branch
  git rebase main
  ```

### Cherry-Picking
- **What it does**: Applies a specific commit from one branch to another.
- **When to use**: When you need a single commit from another branch.
- **Example**:
  ```bash
  git cherry-pick abc1234
  ```

### Hooks
- **What they are**: Scripts that run automatically at key moments (e.g., before a commit).
- **Common hooks**:
  - `pre-commit`: Run tests before allowing a commit.
  - `pre-push`: Check for sensitive data before pushing.

### Real-World Example
A team uses a `pre-commit` hook to enforce commit message conventions. If the message doesn’t follow the format, Git blocks the commit and prompts the developer to fix it.

## Identifying Further Learning Resources

Git is a deep tool, and there’s always more to learn. Here are some next steps:

### Official Documentation
- [Git Documentation](https://git-scm.com/doc) – The definitive reference.
- [GitHub Guides](https://guides.github.com/) – Tutorials for common workflows.

### Community Channels
- **Stack Overflow**: Search for Git-related questions or ask your own.
- **GitHub Discussions**: Engage with open-source projects.
- **Local Meetups**: Look for Git or software development groups.

### Advanced Topics to Explore
- **Git submodules**: Managing multiple repositories as dependencies.
- **Git bisect**: Finding the commit that introduced a bug.
- **Git workflows**: Comparing Git Flow, Trunk-Based Development, etc.

## Key Takeaways
- **Use structured commit messages** (e.g., Conventional Commits) for clarity.
- **Keep branches small and merge often** to avoid conflicts.
- **Never commit sensitive data**—use `.gitignore` and environment variables.
- **Explore advanced techniques** like rebasing, cherry-picking, and hooks.
- **Continue learning** through documentation, communities, and practice.

By following these best practices, you’ll work more efficiently, collaborate more effectively, and avoid common pitfalls. Happy version controlling!

A version control system is software that **records the history of changes** to files (or sets of files) over time. Each time you tell the system to “save” a snapshot, it creates a new, immutable record that you can later retrieve, compare, or roll back to. ### Core Idea in Plain Language - **Snapshot** – Think of a photograph of your project at a particular moment. - **History** – A chronological album of those photographs, each labeled with when it was taken and why. - **Restore** – The ability to replace the current view of your project with any earlier photograph. ### Why Do We Need It? | Situation | Without VCS | With VCS | |-----------|--------------|----------| | **Accidental deletion** | File disappears forever or you must dig through backups. | Retrieve the deleted file from the previous snapshot instantly. | | **Multiple contributors** | Overwrites, lost work, endless “who has the latest version?” emails. | Each change is tracked, merged safely, and attributed to its author. | | **Experimenting** | Fear of breaking the project; you may avoid trying new ideas. | Create a separate line of development (a *branch*) and discard it without harm. | | **Audit & accountability** | Hard to know who changed what and why. | Every change is logged with author, timestamp, and an optional message. | | **Release management** | No clear way to package a specific state for deployment. | Tag a particular commit as a release, guaranteeing reproducibility. | These benefits translate into **greater confidence**, **faster collaboration**, and **more reliable software**—or any collection of files, for that matter. --- ## Centralized vs. Distributed Version Control Version control systems come in two broad families. Understanding the difference helps explain why Git’s distributed model has become dominant. ### 1. Centralized Version Control Systems (CVCS) A centralized system relies on a **single, authoritative server** that holds the master copy of the project. Developers *check out* files, edit them locally, and then *commit* their changes back to the central server. #### Classic Examples - **CVS** (Concurrent Versions System) – early 1990s. - **Subversion (SVN)** – popular in the 2000s. #### How It Works (Simplified Flow) 1. **Checkout** a working copy from the central repository. 2. **Edit** files locally. 3. **Commit** changes back to the central server. 4. **Update** your local copy to incorporate others’ commits. #### Advantages - **Simple mental model** – “One place, one source of truth.” - **Easy access control** – Administrators can manage permissions centrally. #### Drawbacks - **Network dependency** – You cannot commit or view history without a connection to the server. - **Single point of failure** – If the server crashes, the entire team is blocked. - **Limited offline work** – Developers can only view the latest snapshot; they cannot create private histories. ### 2. Distributed Version Control Systems (DVCS) A distributed system, like Git, gives **every clone a full copy of the entire repository**, including its complete history. There is no single “central” server; any clone can act as a source for others. #### Popular Examples - **Git** – created in 2005 for the Linux kernel. - **Mercurial** – another DVCS, similar in philosophy. #### How It Works (Simplified Flow) 1. **Clone** a repository – you receive the whole history. 2. **Commit** locally – changes are saved in your private copy. 3. **Push** or **pull** – exchange commits with other clones when you choose. #### Advantages - **Full offline capability** – you can view history, create branches, and commit without any network. - **Robustness** – If any server fails, any clone can become the new source. - **Flexible workflows** – Teams can adopt centralized, peer‑to‑peer, or hybrid models. #### Drawbacks - **Initial clone size** – The first download can be larger because it includes the whole history. - **Steeper learning curve** – Concepts like *push*, *pull*, and *rebasing* can be confusing at first. ### Why Git Won the Race Git combines **speed**, **data integrity**, and **flexible branching** with a **tiny footprint** for each commit (thanks to clever storage of changes). Its design, originally crafted for a project with thousands of contributors spread around the globe, makes it uniquely suited for both solo developers and massive open‑source communities. --- ## Core Git Terminology (First Encounter) When you start using Git, you’ll repeatedly see a handful of words. Knowing them early prevents confusion later. ### Repository (Repo) A **repository** is the container that holds **all** of your project’s files **and** the complete history of every change. Think of it as the “photo album” for your code. - **Local repository** – The copy on your own computer. - **Remote repository** – A copy hosted on a server (e.g., GitHub, GitLab) that you can share with others. ### Working Directory (or Working Tree) The **working directory** is the set of files you see on disk and edit day‑to‑day. It reflects the state of a particular commit (often the latest one you checked out). ### Commit A **commit** is a **snapshot** of the entire project at a given moment, together with a **commit message** that explains *why* the change was made. Commits form a chain, each pointing to its predecessor, creating the project’s history. - **Commit hash** – A unique 40‑character identifier (e.g., `a1b2c3d4…`) generated from the commit’s contents. - **Commit message** – A short description (ideally imperative, like “Fix login bug”) that helps others understand the purpose of the change. ### Branch A **branch** is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit. It allows you to diverge from the main line of development, work on a feature or experiment, and later bring those changes back together. - **`main` (or `master`)** – The default branch that usually represents the stable, release‑ready code. - **Feature branch** – A temporary branch named after the work you’re doing (e.g., `feature/login-form`). ### Staging Area (Index) Before a commit is created, Git lets you **stage** individual changes. The most common remote name is `origin`, which usually points to the primary shared repository. --- ## Real‑World Snapshots: Seeing the Concepts in Action ### Example 1 – A Solo Writer Using Git Locally *Anna* is drafting a short story. She creates a folder `my‑novel/` and runs `git init` (we’ll cover that command later). 1. **First draft** – She writes the opening paragraph, stages the file (`git add .`), and commits (`git commit -m "Add opening paragraph"`). 2. **Revising** – After a week, she rewrites the opening to be more compelling. Git does not move or copy any of your existing files; it merely creates a hidden folder named **`.git`** that will store all the metadata, objects, and configuration needed to track changes. > **Why “init”?** > The verb “initialize” is short for “set up the initial data structures.” In the earlier chapter on *Installing Git and Initial Configuration* you learned that Git is a **distributed version control system (VCS)**. `git init` is the local counterpart of creating a new project on a remote server—it establishes the *authoritative* source of truth for your project on your own machine. ### What Happens Inside `.git`? The hidden `.git` directory is the heart of every repository. Although you normally never need to look inside it, understanding its purpose helps demystify many later commands. | Sub‑folder / file | Purpose | |-------------------|---------| | `objects/` | Stores **snapshots** (called *objects*) of file contents, identified by SHA‑1 hashes. | | `refs/` | Holds pointers to the **heads** of branches (e.g., `refs/heads/main`). | | `HEAD` | A tiny file that tells Git which branch you’re currently on. | | `config` | Local configuration overrides (e.g., user name, email, merge settings). | | `index` | The **staging area** (also called the *cache*) that records which files are ready to be committed. | Because the folder name begins with a dot (`.`), most operating systems treat it as **hidden**. Visualizing these zones helps you understand what each command does. ``` +-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | Working Directory | <---> | Staging Area ( | <---> | Repository (.git) | | (your files) | add | index) | commit| (history) | +-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+ ``` 1. **Working Directory** – The files you see on disk. They can be edited, renamed, or deleted at any time. 2. **Staging Area** – A hidden snapshot of *exactly* what will be committed next. `git add` copies file contents from the working directory into this area. 3. **Repository** – The permanent, immutable history stored inside `.git`. Each commit adds a new snapshot to this history. When you first run `git init`, the staging area exists (the `index` file) but is empty.
